newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: UN cites delay in delivering food to Iraqi people.
newsitem.headline: UN cites delay in delivering food to Iraqi people.

text.p: The United Nations on Tuesday said it was unlikely that all humanitarian goods would be distributed to the Iraqi people within the six-month period alloted under the so-called oil-for-food plan.

U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan, in a draft report prepared for the Security Council, said because of delays in getting food, medicine and other supplies to Iraq, it was too soon to analyse the impact of the programme.

Consequently, he did not make any recommendations about actions the council might take in June when the six month plan expires, as the first supplies were not due in Iraq until later this month, according to the preliminary report obtained by Reuters.
Several diplomats, however, have speculated that the plan would be renewed by the council in June under similar terms.
At issue is a deal that allows Iraq to sell $2 billion worth of oil over six months to buy humanitarian goods for its people in order to ease the impact of stringent sanctions.
About a third of the revenues would go to victims of the Kuwaiti invasion and to help defray U.N. costs.
Iraq has been under the embargoes since August 1990 when Baghdad's troops invaded Kuwait. The oil-for-food plan went into effect on Dec. 10 but no goods have arrived yet.

Under a 1995 Security Council resolution setting up the plan, Annan was to report to the council after 90 days on how Iraq was implementing the programme and whether the oil revenues were adequate to meet Iraq's humanitarian needs.
But he said that "it appears unlikely that all of the humanitarian goods in the distribution plan will be delivered and distributed within the initial 180 days."
Therefore, he confined the report to analysing the plan to date rather than whether "Iraq had ensured the equitable distribution of supplies" for civilian needs.
Annan said the oil sales, which specially appointed U.N. overseers had to approve, had gone smoothly and Iraq had met the $1 billion target within the first 90 days.

This included approximately 52.3 million barrels sold at an estimated value of $1.07 billion. About 66 percent of the oil went through Iraq's pipelines ot Turkey, the remainder through its port at Mina al-Bakr.
But the approval and execution of the food supplies, while "keeping with commercial practice" proved more complicated and goods took longer to arrive than anticipated.

The United Nations last Friday said that the first food shipments were due at the end of March, although they had been approved on Feb. 14. One vessel carrying 25,350 tons of wheat left France on Feb. 19 but had mechanical trouble and now will not arrive before March 30.
To speed up the implementation Annan also said that the Security Council's sanctions committee had instituted new procedures to expedite approval of food contracts.
U.N. officials and diplomats have blamed the delay on U.N. staff as well as the Security Council's committee. By last week 15 contracts had been approved among 267 submitted.
